newsitem.title: UK: Traffic lights kit gives go-ahead to lovers.
newsitem.headline: Traffic lights kit gives go-ahead to lovers.

text.p: A revolutionary traffic light system which tells couples when they can have sex without the risk of pregnancy could make major inroads into the market for condoms and the pill, its makers claimed Monday.
Unipath, part of Anglo-Dutch consumer giant Unilever, said its new Persona monitoring kit will tell women exactly when they risk getting pregnant, by testing the hormones contained in urine.
"The monitor will indicate a green light when a woman is free to make love without using a contraceptive and a red light on the days on which she is at risk of becoming pregnant," Unipath said.
The company claimed 95 percent reliability for the kit, about the same as for condoms but below the 99 to 100 percent security offered by the pill.
The $77.95 starter kit consists of a small hand-held monitor and 16 test sticks, which are used to build up a picture of a woman's individual cycle in the first month of use.
From then on it asks for only eight tests a month, with a yellow warning light showing when a test is needed.
Unipath said there were millions of women dissatisfied with their choice in contraception and said it anticipated many would adopt Persona as their new method.
British women will be the first to try the kit, which scientists have developed from Unipath's home fertility and pregnancy-testing kits Clearblue and Clearplan.
Franca Tranza, a spokeswoman for the family planning agency Marie Stopes International, welcomed the development as widening the choices open to women.
But she added "it does not mean it will be suitable for everybody. If people are happy with the contraceptive they are using there is no reason to change."
Tranza said Persona will be most attractive to women concerned about side-effects from taking the pill, but warned that "if you opt for that you will be changing to a less secure method."
The makers also warned that the kit, like the pill, cannot protect women against sexually transmitted diseases and the HIV virus.
No one was immediately available for comment at London International Group Plc, the world's largest maker of condoms.
